reason: The sources provide rich, well-corroborated details across multiple independent sites covering Pioneer 10's launch, records, Jupiter flyby, and the Pioneer plaque.
story: Launched in March 1972, Pioneer 10 was humanity's vanguard into deep space. Designed for just a 21-month lifespan, it became the first spacecraft to navigate the hazardous asteroid belt, withstand Jupiter's brutal radiation belts, and reach escape velocity out of the Solar System. Bolted to its antenna strut was a gold-anodized aluminum plaque conceived by Carl Sagan and Frank Drake, bearing diagrams of neutral hydrogen, a 14-pulsar map pinpointing Earth's location, and illustrations of a nude man and woman. Along its path, Pioneer returned the first close-up images of Jupiter and the Great Red Spot. Decades later, an unexplained deceleration known as the Pioneer Anomaly baffled scientists until 2012, when thermal radiation recoil proved to be the cause. Surviving more than 30 years before sending its final transmission in January 2003, Pioneer 10 now drifts silently as a ghost ship toward the constellation Taurus.
angle: Humanity's first interstellar emissary, carrying a cosmic roadmap to Earth and drawings of nude humans, survived lethal Jovian radiation and flew for over 30 years on a mission originally designed to last only 21 months.

claims.claim: Pioneer 10 launched in March 1972 aboard an Atlas-Centaur rocket.
Pioneer 10 became the first spacecraft to traverse the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.
Pioneer 10 was the first human-made spacecraft to fly past Jupiter.
Pioneer 10 was the first artificial object placed on a trajectory to achieve escape velocity from the Solar System.
Pioneer 10 carried a gold-anodized aluminum plaque intended as a message for intelligent extraterrestrial life.
The Pioneer plaque was designed by Carl Sagan and Frank Drake.
The artwork of the human figures on the plaque was drawn by Linda Salzman Sagan.
The plaque depicts nude human figures of a man and a woman.
The plaque includes a map triangulating the position of the Sun using the directions and timing periods of 14 pulsars.
The plaque uses the hyperfine transition of neutral hydrogen to establish fundamental units of length and time in binary notation.
Pioneer 10 passed the Moon just 11 hours after liftoff, making it the fastest human-made object at the time.
Pioneer 10 entered the asteroid belt on July 15, 1972, and safely exited in February 1973.
Pioneer 10 reached closest approach to Jupiter in December 1973, passing within approximately 81,000 to 82,000 miles of the planet.
Pioneer 10 returned more than 500 images of Jupiter and its atmosphere, including views of the Great Red Spot.
Pioneer 10 crossed the orbit of Neptune on June 13, 1983, becoming the first human-built object to venture beyond the major planets.
Pioneer 10 was originally designed for a 21-month mission but continued operating for more than 30 years.
Pioneer 10 sent its final detectable radio signal back to Earth in January 2003.
Pioneer 10 is drifting toward the red giant star Aldebaran in the constellation Taurus, taking an estimated two million years to reach that region.
The spacecraft was powered by SNAP-19 radioisotope thermoelectric generators fueled by plutonium-238.
The mystery of the Pioneer Anomaly was solved in 2012 when researchers proved that heat radiating unevenly from the spacecraft generated a recoil force pushing it toward the Sun.

disputed: The launch date is cited as March 2, 1972, in local Eastern Standard Time (S1, S3, S5) and March 3, 1972, in Coordinated Universal Time (S1, S6); scripts should specify March 2 Eastern Time or March 3 UTC.

The date of Pioneer 10's final signal is given as January 23, 2003, by NASA and Wikipedia (S1, S3), but January 22, 2003, by The Planetary Society (S4); scripts should cite January 23, 2003, or simply late January 2003.

Accounts differ on why the line representing the female pudendal cleft was omitted from the plaque: Carl Sagan attributed it to artistic precedent from classical Greek sculptures and concern over potential NASA censorship, whereas NASA manager Robert Kraemer stated headquarters officials explicitly demanded its removal as a condition for approval; scripts should attribute this as 'according to agency memoirs'.
